items.title: PSA: Beware of old Bitly links taking you to terrible sites
items.content_html:
Internet users really should be careful about link shortening services, as the recent spate of Bitly link hijacking affecting social media accounts demonstrates.

Link shortening services like Bitly are meant to be useful tools, enabling long URLs to be more manageable on social media, such as on X. However, it can also be an attack vector that will catch some users, and major brands, out.

Add in that browser scams tricking Mac users into bypassing Mac security protections is on the rise, and it becomes a really big problem.

Social media accounts for companies including McDonald's, Burger King, and even President Donald Trump, were showing posts with unexpected content changes. They included Bitly URLs that had been redirected to completely different content.

As collected by Cybernews, a McDonald's post from July 2011 suggested users could check out what its team in Sweden did that was "Pretty Cool." However, the preview of the Bitly link in X showed it went to the Wikipedia page for the September 11 attacks.

why would McDonald's Sweden do this https://t.co/zPLESwm4XK

— nyara (@nyaraVT) November 15, 2026

Similarly, a post from Burger King dated July 2011 proposed that readers could find their nearest restaurant via a Bitly link. The X preview showed it was a Wikipedia list of Nazi concentration camps.

Another early tweet from Trump talked about a "clubhouse on the North Sea," with the link going to a Wikipedia entry covering the Epstein Files.

None of the URLs would be anything the brands or Trump would openly link to in such a way. However, they all involve link shortening services and very old social media posts.

Online link rot

The problem is one involving how Bitly treats old links that the service handled. For some reason, not only was it possible for links to expire, but they could also be reused.

In an X post on the matter, posted on Sunday, Bitly admits it had to deal with an issue where "bad actors" were able to repurpose "certain old, inactive links" to send Internet users to other unrelated content.

Earlier today, we identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts. We have suspended the accounts involved and are disabling the affected links. Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future.

— Bitly (@Bitly) November 15, 2026

Bitly insists it has suspended the accounts that did this, and is working to disable those affected links. It also says its Trust and Safety Team is working on the problem to prevent similar instances of link misuse.

Presumably one of the measures it will have to undertake is not expiring links in the first place.

Beware of Bitly

The affair has lessons for both sides of the link equation. For the moment it seems like a problem that pranksters have used to full effect, but it could easily have involved the spread of malware.

For those viewing the Bitly links on social media, carefully check the link preview before clicking it, if available. If there is an obvious disconnect between the account linking the content, the age of the post, and the preview, you probably shouldn't click it.

If you don't have a preview available, Bitly has a link checker, which you can paste a URL into to see the final destination. You could also add a plus symbol to the end of a Bitly URL to see the destination.

For people sharing links online, this serves as a reminder that using intermediary services like Bitly must be done with caution. You are handing over control of your links to another service which could be the victim of a breach or simply die overnight.

It's a trade-off, losing control in favor of a more easily shared URL. But, in cases like this, it's something that can eventually become a problem long in the future.

items.title: 'Schmigadoon!' and 'Widow's Bay' earn Grammy nominations for Apple
items.content_html:
The 2027 Grammy Awards nominations include one nod for recent Apple TV hit "Widow's Bay," and another for the show Apple cancelled, "Schmigadoon!"

Despite Apple TV cancelling "Schmigadoon!" after two seasons had aired — and a third had been written — the musical has gone on to greater success on stage. It has already won multiple Tony Awards, and now has been nominated for a Grammy.

The 2027 Grammy Award nominations have just been announced and include:

  • Best Musical Theater Album: Schmigadoon!
  • Best Score Soundtrack For Visual Media: Widow's Bay

Apple Music has already added a Grammys 2027 nomination playlist.

The "Schmigadoon!" stage musical is based in part on the first season of the Apple TV version. Back in June 2026 when it won Tony Awards including Best Musical, its producer called out the streamer for the cancellation decision.

"I think I should start by thanking Apple TV for cancelling the third season of 'Schmigadoon!' the TV show," said Christine Schwarzmann, "because without them we couldn't have picked it up and ran with it."

It's because of "Schmigadoon!" that Apple became an EGOT winner, the recipient of Emmys, Grammys, Oscars, and Tony Awards. But in September 2026, it was "Widow's Bay" that led Apple TV to record-breaking Emmy wins.

Those Emmys includied ones for Outstanding Music Composition and Outstanding Music Supervision. Now the show has been nominated for a Grammy for best soundtrack score.

The winners will be announced on Sunday, February 7, 2027. For the first time in 54 years, the Grammys will be screened on ABC.

items.title: Video Podcasts are coming soon to tvOS
items.content_html:
Apple is finally catching up with the trend of video podcasts, by adding a video podcasts section to the Apple TV in Monday's tvOS 27.3 developer beta.

Video podcasts have been growing in popularity in recent years, with both YouTube and Spotify hosting large numbers of them. Now, Apple wants to become a bigger presence in the market, including on Apple TV.

A video podcasts section will be added to the Apple TV on Monday, as part of the developer beta, reports the New York Times. The section will be available to all testers and will make it easier for users to watch that content.

This was a previously known change, with podcast updates previously revealed to be coming to tvOS 27 at some point.

It's not the only thing Apple has planned, as it apparently wants to increase the number of video podcasts shown in its Podcasts app.

The Podcasts app was updated earlier in 2026, with the addition of native video playback powered by HTTP Live Streaming, or HLS.

"We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them - the small screens, big screens," said Apple VP Oliver Schusser who manages services including podcasts. The intention is claimed to be to help improve discovery for users, and for content creators to reach a new audience.

Schusser insists that it wasn't done in a way that would "financially benefit" Apple.

items.title: iPhone 20 Pro will resemble a more rounded iPhone Air
items.content_html:
A new report from a leaker with only a mixed track record, says that the 20th anniversary iPhone will use the same all-glass design as the iPhone Air.

Leaker Fixed Focus Digital has previously claimed that the base or regular iPhone 20 will be predominantly the same design as the iPhone Air. Now they are back saying that the iPhone 20 Pro will be as well.

Specifically, the leaker says (in translation) that the iPhone 20 Pro will be made "of the same glass material as the iPhone Air series." However, it will also have "a more pronounced curvature, delivering a four-curved surface effect."

As well as being identical to their base iPhone 20 rumor, this claim does back up one from another leaker. In May 2026, leaker Digital Chat Station said that Apple was planning a quad-curved OLED display for the iPhone 20 Pro.

Digital Chat Station has a stronger track record than Fixed Focus Digital, but they are both leakers on Weibo. The Chinese social media platform tends to have more repeats of existing rumors than it does new information.

Given how this new leak about the iPhone 20 Pro is so like previous ones about the iPhone 20, it may well be another case of one report being picked up and repeated. That said, it wouldn't be a surprise if Apple did this design, so the rumor could equally well be a reasoned assumption.

items.title: PROLED MacBook Pro review: Great hardware, maybe wait for M7
items.content_html:
The 16-inch MacBook Pro finally goes OLED, with the new PROLED XDR screen stealing the show. Touch, fortunately, isn't overdone, or necessary at all.

Apple spent years perfecting the MacBook Pro's mini-LED screen. It was bright, sharp, and genuinely very good.

Not good enough for Cupertino, apparently.

The new 16-inch MacBook Pro moves to a tandem OLED panel Apple calls PROLED XDR. On paper, it is the biggest display leap the Mac has ever taken.

It arrives with a touch screen, a Dynamic Island, and a rebuilt cooling system. There is a lot to unpack here.

ProductApple 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display
Base price$3,399
ChipApple M5 Pro or M5 Max
CPU18-core (6 super, 12 performance), per Apple's spec
GPU20-core (M5 Pro); 32-core or 40-core (M5 Max)
Neural Engine16-core, with GPU Neural Accelerators
Unified memoryUp to 64GB (M5 Pro); up to 128GB (M5 Max)
Memory bandwidth307GB/s (M5 Pro); up to 614GB/s (M5 Max)
StorageUp to 4TB (M5 Pro); up to 16TB (M5 Max)
Display16.3-inch PROLED XDR tandem OLED, touch, 3472 x 2266, 254 ppi
Brightness1,000 nits sustained, 2,000 nits peak (HDR and SDR)
Contrast10,000,000:1
Refresh rateProMotion, adaptive 10Hz to 120Hz
ColorP3 and Adobe RGB, 1 billion colors, True Tone
Battery100Wh; up to 24h video (M5 Pro), 22h (M5 Max)
Ports3x Thunderbolt 5 (120Gb/s), HDMI, SDXC, MagSafe 3, 3.5mm
WirelessApple N1, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread
Camera12MP Center Stage, Desk View, 1080p
AudioSix-speaker, force-cancelling woofers, three-mic array
Dimensions (inches)0.63 x 14.0 x 9.62
Weight4.0 lb (M5 Pro); 4.1 lb (M5 Max)
ColorsSpace Black, Silver

MacBook Pro 16-inch review: A lighter, bolder redesign

This is the first real redesign of the Pro chassis in years. You feel it the moment you pick it up.

The 16-inch model now weighs 4.0 pounds, down from 4.7. That is nearly three-quarters of a pound gone, which is a lot at this size.

MacBook Pro review: From top to bottom - MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro

We got similar weight reductions on the 13-inch model too, dropping from 3.5 pounds to 3.0 pounds.

The display borders are slimmer, too. The screen feels like it floats closer to the edges than before.

Apple has also brought the iPhone's Dynamic Island to the Mac. It's a choice that has induced internet drama. On the surface, the logic for having it on MacBook Pro is less obvious than on a phone. More on Dynamic Island in a bit.

The headline change, though, is touch. Intricuit and Modbook aside, this is the first Apple-made MacBook you can prod, pinch, and scroll with a finger.

Apple built the touch sensor into the panel itself, rather than layering it on top.

The MacBook Pro has been a workhorse machine, rarely shying away from power just because of its portable design. After just toting it around for a few days, the upgraded design is well worth it.

MacBook Pro review: The new MacBook Pro models have recessed feet which helps reduce their height on your desk

That weight difference is noticeable from the moment you pick up the MacBook Pro, and it carries through to the user experience. Interestingly, the bottom feet are recessed into the lower case, so the laptop doesn't sit as high on your desk, and typing doesn't feel as bouncy.

When you open the laptop, you feel how much thinner the top is.

The premium feel has not been lost, despite being thinner and lighter. If you are a photographer, developer, or any other power user that is carrying this around regularly, the lighter design makes a good case for itself.

When Apple launched the new iPhone 18 Pro, one of the new changes was a smaller Dynamic Island. On the Mac, Apple went from a notch to the hole-punch camera, and it's far more noticeable than the iterative change on iPhone.

MacBook Pro review: The notch on the old MacBook Pro took up so much space and menu items had to go around it

The old notch was larger and took up a lot of menu bar space. We'd frequently have items wrapping around to the other side in the menu bar.

By moving to the smaller Dynamic Island, there's room in the menu bar. And, it's also the home for Live Activities.

The Live Activity UI has so good on mobile, it's a little surprising that it took this long for Apple to bring it to the Mac. It does take up more space, but it's the most elegant way to keep track of timers, media, or see system controls.

MacBook Pro Review: The Dynamic Island is a great upgrade

Items shrink down and they expand when you go over them with your mouse or hold on them with your finger. Older machines get this too with an update to macOS, but it works better with the camera cutout than the larger notch.

Speaking of the touch input, your mileage is certainly going to vary. It's not a must-have feature for most, but there's also no reason to get mad that it exists. Use it if you want, but there isn't and probably won't ever be a mandate to use it.

Apple has updated in places to support touch, but it isn't an overhaul of the system that puts touch first. It's small stuff, like holding on an item in the dock to open the contextual menu.

You can swipe up and down to scroll, drag things around between windows, and pinch and zoom into photos. Working with media was particularly effective with the touch controls.

MacBook Pro review: Some elements expand and react to your touch, like the stoplight window buttons

The stoplight icons for window management work great and expand as you touch and hold on them so you can still see, but some menus are too small. There's definitely still work and polish that needs to be done.

More often than not, a trackpad or mouse is just as fast, or faster, than using touch.

This is probably the right approach though, because macOS doesn't get a radical change that changes everything about it to optimize for touch. Instead you get the same, excellent macOS experience with an optional bonus layer of touch for those that want to use it.

What we would like to see is a little less bounce in the screen when the touchscreen is being used. It's still a little bouncy, so perhaps this is where the extra half-pound that got shaved off would have made a difference.

MacBook Pro 16-inch review: The PROLED XDR display

The PROLED XDR display is why you buy this machine, and is the best display Apple has ever put in a laptop. While Apple's mini LED backlit display is fantastic, the PROLED display is superb.

Tandem OLED stacks two OLED layers to push out more light. The result is a 16.3-inch screen at 3472 by 2266, holding the familiar 254 pixels per inch.

MacBook Pro review: The new MacBook Pro with PROLED

Peak brightness climbs to 2,000 nits, and for both HDR and SDR content. The old mini-LED panel managed 1,600 nits, and only for HDR. This goes brighter, and does it everywhere.

Contrast is the bigger jump. It leaps from 1,000,000 to one on mini-LED, up to 10,000,000 to one here.

OLED's per-pixel blacks are the reason why. Dark scenes lose the faint glow that even good mini-LED tends to leave behind.

Apple has also added Adobe RGB alongside the usual P3. Photographers and print designers will clock that straight away.

MacBook Pro review: The MacBook Pro comes in 14-inch and 16-inch models

ProMotion carries over, with an adaptive range now stretching from 10Hz to 120Hz. The nano-texture glass option remains for anyone battling glare.

It is, simply, a stunning screen. Even going from mini LED, the PROLED looks fantastic in use.

It's a gorgeous display with inky black and vivid peak brightness. Colors pop and whether you're editing content or consuming media, it looks great.

MacBook Pro review: The PROLED display looks great, especially with HDR content

There's a lot of little changes that Apple put into this display that pay off as you use it. For example, it's brighter when in sunlight but also has lower reflectivity.

We've tested the new MacBook Pro outside, in some harsh living room sunlight, and in the studio lighting and the display was always legible. It felt like it had ample brightness and generally less glare.

The nano-texture version could cut down those reflections even further. We didn't test that here, but this time Apple says that the texture is etched directly into the glass.

OLED on MacBook Pro for the first time, and Pulse Width Modulation

As it pertains to the OLED display in the new MacBook Pro, Pulse Width Modulation is what Apple uses to regulate the brightness of individual color cells in the eye displays.

An incandescent bulb that can dim throws off fewer photons when at a lower wattage. It does not turn off quickly and strobe — it just emits fewer photons because of the lower power.

In any OLED display, brightness control and color mixing is accomplished by turning individual color cells on and off very quickly. If full power, constantly, is being applied to a color cell, then that cell is "on time" or at a 100% duty cycle, and is fully bright.

Pulse width modulation and duty cycle example - credit circuitdigest.com

While there is an overall screen refresh frequency factor to consider as it pertains to health, in short, given a fixed frequency, to reduce the brightness, the color cell is extremely rapidly turned on and off.

This is complex, so we're going to simplify it a bit. A 50% duty cycle has the cell on or off half of the time, and is about half the brightness. It also effectively strobes the user at a different frequency than the display as a whole is doing.

Pulse Width Modulation has been used in OLED iPhones since the iPhone X. It has always been a health concern at some level, to some people.

If you haven't had sensitivity with your iPhone or iPad before, that doesn't necessarily mean that you'll be fine with the MacBook Pro.

For the new MacBook Pro, it's not the entire field of vision, but it is a wide one. The pulse width modulation, which is not the same as the screen refresh rate, is running at 240Hz on the new MacBook Pro, with a 56% flicker amplitude. This is the same as it is on modern iPhones, but it is also on a much larger screen, and as such, a wider field of vision at relatively close range.

Sensitivity to strobing lights is also aggravated by fatigue of any sort, diet, time of exposure to the strobing and a host of other situations. If you're well-rested, you may not be sensitive to strobing lights.

If you've skipped a meal, are pulling an all-nighter in front of your MacBook Pro, and didn't get any sleep the previous night, that's about the worst-case scenario.

Our advice is the same as it has always been. If you start feeling strange in any way while using the new MacBook Pro, or for that matter, anything with a screen, stop using it. Talk to your doctor about it.

And if you know you have a sensitivity to it, do not buy this MacBook Pro. If it develops in the first few days of use, take advantage of Apple's generous return policy.

And, as always, just because you're not having an issue, doesn't mean that it's not a problem.

MacBook Pro 16-inch review: Thermals and performance

The 16-inch Pro has long been the Mac that runs hottest under sustained load. A redesigned thermal architecture aims squarely at that.

MacBook Pro review: The logo etched into the metal on the bottom of the MacBook Pro

Apple is light on specifics, as ever. At release the company highlighted that redesigned thermal system rather than hard numbers. The promise is more sustained performance with less fan noise. For video editors and developers, that matters more than a headline chip score.

But, we couldn't tell if it actually makes a difference or not. The longer jobs we use to test pro hardware completed in the same time within the margin of error for multiple runs. Acoustic testing while getting hammered with work was also within the margin of error, using our faithful Kanomax meter we've been using for years.

So, in practice, that's all about the same as the previous M5 Pro and M5 Max offerings. As with the previous model, exporting a 15-minute 4K video file out of Final Cut Pro wasn't enough to get the fans kicking in beyond a mild hum part way through the task.

More intensive local AI tasks, rendering complex models in Blender, or working in Spatial video are going to be the activities to get these fans humming.

Also the same, is the chip choice. Regarding those chips, the same M5 Pro and the M5 Max are here. Both use an 18-core CPU, with six super cores and twelve performance cores, per Apple's spec.

The M5 Pro pairs that with a 20-core GPU. The M5 Max steps up to 32 or 40 GPU cores, and as much as 128GB of memory.

Memory bandwidth tops out at 614GB/s on the fastest Max. That is the part that feeds heavy GPU and AI work.

Apple's own figures claim the M5 Pro is up to 10.9 times faster than the M1 Pro, with "up to" doing a lot of work in that claim. The M5 Max is pitched at up to 12 times the M1 Max.

Sure, that's all fine and good. We're sure that Apple got those results somewhere. Your mileage will vary, based on your own workflows, like always.

We're not going to bomb you with benchmarks. They're the same as last time, within less than a percent.

MacBook Pro review: Dock on the MacBook Pro

The read here is that you already run an M-series Pro or Max, the screen is the upgrade here, not the silicon. We think that the redesigned cooling system is more Apple-serving than user-serving, and exists more to keep heat off the screen, than keep the chips cooler.

MacBook Pro 16-inch review: Battery, ports, and audio

Battery holds at the usual 100 watt-hours, the legal ceiling for a laptop. Apple rates the M5 Pro at up to 24 hours of video, and the M5 Max at 22. Our practical testing bore that out.

MacBook Pro review: On the right side, the MacBook Pro has an SDXC card reader, a Thunderbolt 5 port, and an HDMI port

The port selection is unchanged, which is no bad thing at all. You get three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, an SDXC slot, MagSafe 3, and a headphone jack.

Thunderbolt 5 runs up to 120Gb/s, with DisplayPort 2.1 for high-end external screens. The M5 Max can drive up to four of them. This remains the same as the previous generation.

MacBook Pro review: The left side has a MagSafe 3 charging port, two Thunderbolt 5 ports, an a headphone jack

Wireless moves to Apple's own N1 chip, with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The webcam stays a 12MP Center Stage unit with Desk View.

Audio steps up to a six-speaker system with force-cancelling woofers. On a laptop people actually watch movies on, that is a welcome touch.

MacBook Pro 16-inch review: Come for the screen, maybe wait for M7

This is the most exciting MacBook Pro in a long time. The PROLED XDR display alone makes it feel like a genuine new chapter.

MacBook Pro review: MacBook Pro is now more portable than ever

Come for that screen, and the rest of the spec sheet will not let you down. The lighter body and (slightly) better speakers only sweeten the deal.

There is a sensible case for patience, though. This is a first-generation OLED, a first touch screen, and a thermal redesign, all at once. The M5 chip is also not even a step from the last version without the touch screen, it's exactly the same.

So if your current Pro still serves you well, the M7 version that we're expecting in November 2027 or so may iron out the early quirks. The display will be just as spectacular, and maybe the new cooling system will get a tune-up with a vapor chamber heat sink that may actually reduce internal temperatures.

But if you are buying today, this is a wonderful machine. Just go in knowing you are paying a first-generation premium to be early.

MacBook Pro 16-inch review - Pros

  • PROLED XDR is the best laptop display yet, anywhere
  • Lighter body, slimmer borders, better audio
  • "Redesigned thermals" but the verdict is still out on this

MacBook Pro 16-inch review - Cons

  • Bouncy touchscreen still
  • Pulse width modulation may be an issue
  • Price premium on top of already hiked prices

Score: 4 out of 5

We hope that Apple keeps around both PROLED and mini LED versions of the MacBook Pro. We've already heard rumblings that they won't, but we'll see how that goes in the fullness of time.

Just the same, the new 2026 MacBook Pro is a very nice machine. The slimmer enclosure and less weight make a giant difference, and so does the new, and gorgeous, screen.

What it does not deliver, is increased performance versus the previous model. If you've got the previous M5 Pro or M5 Max, you won't get work done faster. If you're coming from an older MacBook Pro, it's a nice upgrade, albeit at a cost.

If all you really need is performance, either skip this generation and wait for that M7 model, or get the previously available model without the PROLED premium.

Either way, you get great power, a great screen, and all-day battery life.

Where to buy MacBook Pro 16-inch PROLED

Apple's 16-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display is on sale now at popular Apple resellers. Amazon carries the retail configurations, while B&H, Expercom, and Adorama are selling both retail and CTO models.

Our 16-inch MacBook Pro PROLED Price Guide has a detailed breakdown of the best offers and latest availability across the line.

items.title: iPhone 20 Pro camera rumored to use a faster 17nm imaging processor
items.content_html:
The iPhone 20 Pro will have an upgraded camera sensor, and it appears Apple will be refreshing the chip and circuitry driving the imaging module.

Camera upgrades are big news when it comes to new iPhone models, such as the introduction of a variable aperture sensor. However, sometimes the changes on the way are smaller, and don't necessarily provide users with more resolution or other cool features.

In one rumor post from Ice Universe on Weibo, the iPhone 20 Pro will have a new main camera. Specifically, it will be using a "new 17nm logic process sensor."

The leaker doesn't explain what will actually change with this 17-nanometer update, but future rumors should help clarify what the improvements are.

A circuitry change

The modern iPhone camera system is very complex and requires its own chips to handle specific functions. For example, the camera module stack has to be able to quickly capture the data pulled from the sensor right after it's been taken.

This is a very high-speed procedure, and relies on components attached directly to the sensor. It would be too slow if the A-series chip in the iPhone had to handle that task.

Then there are features like Apple Reference Image, which requires a secure boot of the sensor and cryptographic signing of pixel data. This is done immediately after capture, and before the operating system touches the generated image.

A new chip may also mean even faster communications, potentially increasing video frame rates or even a faster burst mode.

While Weibo leakers don't have the best reputation when it comes to rumor accuracy, Ice Universe is one of the better ones. They tend to have a decent track record for Apple-specific leaks.

items.title: 'Slow Horses' will continue with unexpected ninth and tenth season order
items.content_html:
Despite rumors of Apple TV hit "Slow Horses" coming to an end, industry sources report that it's been given two further seasons.

The sixth season of spy thriller "Slow Horses" concluded on Apple TV in October 2026 with a teaser for the following season. But then star Olivia Cooke, who plays Sid Baker, said the show was to end with its eighth season.

Specifically, she said that she was currently "shooting the last season," and that this was what she had been told. Plus she said that the case and crew were "melancholy, distracted," because of the impending end.

However, Deadline magazine now reports that Apple has ordered two further seasons. That will bring the show up to ten, which is unprecedented for an Apple TV series.

It also brings the show to having more seasons than there are books in Mick Herron's "Slough House" series of novels. At present there are nine full novels, with the most recent being 2025's "Clown Town."

However, the sixth book's setting in snow-bound Wales was considered too expensive to produce. So season six dramatized both it, "Joe Country," and the following novel, "Slough House."

This means that the production team is currently filming the latest of the full novels. Mick Herron has written five novellas which have just been collected into one volume called "Watch the Quiet Snow."

There is no further information about either production or streaming dates for any of the remaining seasons. Based on the show's previous releases, though, those seasons should see it airing until 2030.

Since the show began in 2022, that means it will have run for eight years. Apple TV's first prestige hit, "The Morning Show," will also have run for eight years when it concludes in 2027, but it will only have had five seasons.

items.title: New Apple TV 4K expanded memory is out of reach for developers
items.content_html:
The new version of the Apple TV 4K has more memory than ever before. However, game and app developers aren't able to take advantage of the increased RAM capacity.

The 2026 update to the Apple TV is out, with its upgrades including the A19 and double the RAM at eight gigabytes. They sound like much-needed improvements for the set-top box for developers, who now have more processing performance at their disposal.

However, while it's one thing for Apple to increase the memory of a device, it's another for developers to actually be able to use it at all. Though there's eight gigabytes available, it seems that an app can only use two gigabytes at the most.

In testing by 9To5Mac, tvOS will automatically force-quit an app if it uses more than two gigabytes. This happens both on the third-generation Apple TV, equipped with four gigabytes of RAM, and the 8-gigabyte fourth-generation model.

Business as usual, sadly

For the previous model, having a 2GB limit for apps makes sense, due to tvOS itself requiring some headroom to function in the first place. With an expansion of memory, you would expect the allocatable amount to increase at the same time.

As it stands, there's no change for developers, who have the same limitations as before. Indeed, developers making apps for Apple's other hardware, such as an iPhone, can run into similar constraints and operating system reactions to high usage levels.

For the most part, streaming media apps don't tend to need that much memory to function. The bulk of the work is simply downloading a video stream, handling the codec, and displaying it for the user.

It is more of a problem for game developers, with intensive graphics typically using up a lot of memory. A higher memory usage could've enabled more high-fidelity graphics to be seen on the Apple TV.

While there was hope for gaming to benefit from the Apple TV upgrade and give more life to the set-top box, the memory limitation makes that a harder reality to achieve.

But why?

It is unclear exactly why Apple has decided to hold back the memory usage for this generation. Apple hasn't said outright why this is the case at all, but there could be some reasons.

For a start, the inclusion of Siri AI support may have something to do with it. When Apple rolled out Apple Intelligence, it required an iPhone 15 Pro at a minimum, which had 8GB of memory.

While Apple's more advanced models require at least 12GB in Apple devices to run, the Apple TV arguably doesn't need that much. At most, it will use Siri AI for queries, not other AI processing tasks.

That is somewhat confirmed by the addition of Siri AI support on the 2021 Apple TV 4K. With 4GB of memory, it makes sense that it should be able to handle Siri AI queries, since it will hand things over to a paired Siri AI-enabled device nearby.

It's also entirely plausible that Apple hasn't raised the per-app memory allowance because it wants more Apple TV 4K models out there beforehand.

If Apple did include support, a developer releasing a game that requires more than 2GB of memory will encounter slow sales at first for the Apple TV 4K. At least until enough people have upgraded their devices to the newer model.

There's also the small chance that Apple decided not to bother with the upgrade at launch at all because it wasn't a high-enough priority. It's doubtful that Apple simply "forgot" about making the change, but it may have its reasons to do so.

items.title: New Apple health study wants to find out how much you trust AI
items.content_html:
Apple has launched a year-long research project into how people trust AI and use it for health advice, since users keep turning to chatbots despite repeated examples of dangerous results.

It's hardly a secret that AI gets things wrong, but still there are cases such as ChatGPT dissuading a pastor from getting his cardiac issue attended to. Giving your health data to ChatGPT is an all-round bad idea, yet it hasn't been blocked from being connected to Apple Health.

Now Apple has launched what it's calling the Apple Health AI Usage Study to examine how users work with health AI chatbots. It's intended to help with making AI health more responsible.

"At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding," Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement. "Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life."

"Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation," she continued, "and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey."

The study is being conducted in collaboration with the OpenEvidence clinical AI platform. Through its study app, Apple is looking for eligible participants and will cap the study at 200,000 people.

To be eligible, users must be US residents and aged 21 or over. They must also have an iPhone 15 Pro or later, running iOS 26 or later, and specifically have Apple Intelligence enabled.

The participants will then be asked to optionally share certain health readings from their iPhone or Apple Watch. They will also be directed to ask what are described as everyday health questions, as well as explore more complex medical information.

"Patients and clinicians are both turning to Al, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds," Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, said in Apple's announcement. "When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly."

"Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we'll get there," he continued.

During the research period, the study app will look for what Apple calls concerning questions. It will then prompt the user to consult with a doctor.

To that end, the study is also concerned with how to use AI to best help users prepare for clinical appointments with their doctors.

Apple has already committed to AI with its recent Health app revamp. It's designed to provide guidance to users over both their general health and the best fitness activities to pursue.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: Unhinged robots and commentator curses
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, iPhone Duo robots may change the reviewing process, and Murphy's Law is alive and well when anyone talks about tech CEOs.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

Unhinged reviews

It's been a few weeks since the first reviews of the iPhone Duo came out. However, while the opinions of the reviews are one thing, there's another thing that is far more interesting.

There's been so much focus on the hinge that it's eclipsing pretty much everything else about the smartphone. To be fair, it's the headline feature, and so it's going to draw a lot of attention.

That attention hasn't been great, exactly. Since launch, we've been plagued by social media posts of a mystery screen break seemingly caused by a weak component in the hinge mechanism.

We've also seen one component maker threaten legal action for unqualified accusatory opinions.

But when it comes to the hinge in a reviewing sense, some outlets decided to do things differently. No bombastic damage-fueled videos, but instead checking that the hinge will work for the lifetime of the device.

Not by using it for a long time, though. More by performing as many actuations of that hinge as possible.

This week, CNET revealed the details of the iPhone Duo's endurance test on a custom rig that opens and closes the smartphone. After over 440,000 folds, the display was still unfolding, with the hinge getting about 95% of the way open.

That's well over the number of times you would expect to open and close the iPhone Duo if you owned it for ten years.

It's not the only outlet to attempt something like this. Joanna Stern's New Things did something similar, attaching a motorized rig to the iPhone Duo. Running at 17 folds per minute, it achieved over 32,000 folds across four nights with "no noticeable deterioration."

This is all activity that goes beyond the usual routine for a review. Even bigger outlets with the funding and the knowledge base for destruction testing don't bother to go down this route of inquiry.

To be fair, it's borderline consumer testing at this stage.

It does, however, raise a question that affects me. Since things like Stern's relatively minimal test rig exist, should other publications consider doing similar electronic projects to do similar repetitive testing when the product hype allows it?

Am I going to have to learn basic electronics and work out how to code something for an Arduino? Do I have to get the 3D printer up and running for something other than plastic desk figurines and replicas of guns from Destiny 2?

I don't think I need to do that just yet. But if the reviewing industry is going to continue this sort of testing, it'll be another thing to invest my spare time into learning.

Goddamnit, Jensen

Readers may be aware of the Sunday Reboot posted two weeks ago that took aim at OpenAI's Sam Altman. His commentary about how your Mac's RAM was wasting away when it should be used by AI companies was not taken that well.

It turns out that when you put a CEO's feet to the flames, they can sometimes feel it.

Altman tried to perform damage control, renaming himself temporarily to "Ram Altman" on X and declaring that he had argued for a ramp-up of memory production for a "long time."

It's a response from the OpenAI chief that is a bit flippant, but really the only healer here is time. Or at least, the gradual failure of human memory.

However, AI CEO foot-in-mouth recovery aside, that column also included something that should be addressed this week. Namely that somehow I have been afflicted by the Commentator's Curse.

Early on in the piece, I discuss how CEO pronouncements can go wrong, due to being made by out-of-touch rich people. That point still stands in general, though.

The problem is that I pointed to the relatively sane comments made by Nvidia's Jensen Huang about paying a billionaire's tax. He was OK with handing over the cash, which is certainly the opposite of what others had said.

At the time, Jensen seemed like a CEO who was relatively normal. Sure, he had a shiny jacket like he was cosplaying someone from The Matrix, but he didn't appear to have any massively weird beliefs, or at least didn't express them in public.

Alas, that was not to last. Almost as if the universe decided my comments wouldn't go unpunished, Jensen was suddenly accused of having an affair with a person accused of being a Chinese spy.

Just for good measure, it wasn't the only affair, either. Embroiled in a massive scandal, Huang was then forced to resign in disgrace.

It's not the end of things for him, either, as he now faces scrutiny by the U.S. government over the whole Chinese spy thing. It also leaves his legacy at Nvidia tainted, as the company seeks to stabilize the ship.

At the very least, he gets to spend the rest of his life with massive wealth and the hope that the glare from the media dies down at some point.

The shortlist of "CEOs who seem normal and haven't done anything doolally yet" is now a bit shorter.

I'm now watching John Ternus as one of the last on the list, quietly hoping there aren't any skeletons in that Apple-shaped closet.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed Apple's cursing challenges, as well as how the new Apple Watch Live Rewind and Siri Recaps being a step towards an episode of "Black Mirror."

items.title: Apple TV+ 'Slow Horses' faces the glue factory after eight seasons
items.content_html:
Fans of the Apple TV+ thriller "Slow Horses" may not continue past season 8, because it will have caught up with the book series.

Editor's note: Despite Colman's remarks, Slow Horses has been renewed through Season 10. The update is here.

Apple confirmed back in September that there would be an eighth season of the Emmy and BAFTA Award-winning spy drama "Slow Horses." However, it seems improbable that it will continue beyond that season for a long time, if at all.

Speaking to The Times, Olivia Cooke said "I am shooting the last season." Cooke, who plays "Sid Baker" on the show, added "never say never" about the warning, since it's what she was told.

The show felt like it was ending, with a "melancholy, distracted" cast and crew seemingly mourning the show's end.

Apple hasn't confirmed it will be the last season, or if there will be future episodes on the way.

Last legs?

The problem "Slow Horses" faces is one involving source material.

Season eight will be adapting "Clown Town" from the "Slough House" book series by Mick Herron. That book was released in 2025, and is the most recent in the series, meaning there's nothing newer to base the show on.

Herron has said there is an intention to continue the story with more books. But, since books can take a long time to write and get published, that can be a long time.

Apple could go down the route of "Game of Thrones" and have the show's story branch off from the books. Though, based on the reaction of fans, that didn't go down well at all.

There's also the possibility of resting the show until more books are available. Though a pause can also be taken as an opportunity by Apple to end the adaptation completely.

Mercifully, there's still some time before fans have to deal with the possible end of the show. Apple TV+ started streaming season six of the show in September, with season 7 probably arriving in 2027.

items.title: Face ID & telephoto lens are coming to iPhone Duo, eventually
items.content_html:
While the timetable isn't clear, Apple is reportedly working on adding Face ID to the iPhone Duo. However, the effective engineering deadline for the late 2027 refresh is coming soon, and the feature may not make the cut.

Apple reportedly has two main priorities for the second-generation iPhone Duo. Those are, sensibly, adding Face ID, and adding an Action Button. We've spoken about the Action Button before, and the most likely implementation is a combination with the camera control button.

But, the loudest complaints we've heard about the model is about the lack of Face ID. A report on Sunday morning by Mark Gurman claims that prototypes exist with Face ID, with integration into having the VCSEL for the biometrics on the outer display.

The hardware, codenamed V78, is nearing the final design stages before first prototypes are assembled and test production starts. As such, Gurman claims that Apple is running out of time for proper integration and inclusion in the 2027 update to the device.

Other goals for future generations include a telephoto camera lens, and reducing the thickness and weight of the unit. He also notes that customer feedback about it, other than what Apple already had on its roadmap that overlaps, shouldn't be expected until the iPhone Duo 3.

items.title: Lightweight Apple Glasses rumored for WWDC 2027 reveal
items.content_html:
Apple could finally announce its smart glasses during WWDC 2027 with privacy-focused features built around the Secure Exclave and Siri AI.

Apple's smart glasses, which AppleInsider has previously dubbed Apple Glass or Apple Vision, have been rumored for years. With the latest products like Apple Watch and HomeView being built around Secure Exclave technology, the pitch for smart glasses is coming into focus.

According to the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, Apple is expected to announce the Siri AI-powered smart glasses during WWDC 2027. They would launch later in the year.

Current prototypes of the smart glasses have oval lenses with cameras flush to the frame. Also, a proprietary magnetic connector on the left arm lets testers use the glasses easily while charging.

It isn't clear if charging while in use will be a feature at launch. The frames are reportedly thinner than Meta's current offering as well.

Expect more on Apple's smart glasses strategy as we approach WWDC 2027 in June. That timetable isn't set in stone, but it is allegedly the current goal.

Apple's Vision

It has become increasingly clear that Apple wants to preserve its privacy image even as it announces AI products that watch, listen, and report on the world around you. The Secure Exclave is central to that feature set and messaging.

Live Rewind is a controversial feature that doesn't record any audio to provide a transcript

On Apple Watch, the Secure Exclave is used for Audio Intelligence features like Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Those tools never actually "capture" or "record" audio in the traditional sense, but analyze data from environment audio to power the features.

The Secure Exclave is a processing unit separate from the main system and nothing can be extracted from it, even by hacking into the main CPU. No audio files are saved or recoverable, thus Apple is able to get around the legal definition of "recording." Though, that hasn't been tested in court just yet.

Apple's HomeView also uses a Secure Exclave for processing audio and video feeds. The device authenticates the user based on visible users in the field of the camera and the voice recognition in the environment.

Like on Apple Watch, no audio or video is recorded, just referenced by the AI tools for authentication purposes. However, Apple's complex system still allows the camera to be used for FaceTime calls through special permission structures.

Visual data from AirPods or Apple smart glasses could appear in Siri Recaps

All of this makes perfect sense for Apple's smart glasses strategy. The company will likely lean in hard on not making "pervert glasses," which is the nickname given to Meta's Ray-Ban glasses that have been the center of so much abuse.

Google's Android XR glasses line will face similar problems. They appear to have similar functionality to Meta's glasses with minimal promises to privacy preservation.

With Samsung's upcoming line of smart glasses, users are able to capture video and photos with the glasses, but a recording light will be visible and allegedly can't be covered or removed. It remains to be seen if these privacy protections and promises not to train on user AI visual data will be enough.

Apple's approach, on the other hand, already has years of groundwork laid around provable privacy and security features found on iPhone. Also, by announcing Audio Intelligence on Apple Watch and the authentication features in Apple HomeVeiw first, Apple is preparing the market for the camera glasses that are somehow different from the much maligned pervert glasses.

AirPods with Cameras are expected to arrive ahead of Apple's smart glasses with a similar feature set.

It isn't yet known if Apple intends to let users capture video, audio, or photos from their version of smart glasses or camera-equipped AirPods. If I were Apple, I would pitch them as cameras for AI, not the user, and the perfectly good iPhone camera in your pocket will do the trick for capturing a moment.

Hindsight is 20/20

The newsletter is fairly confident in its information on the potential release and strategy around Apple smart glasses. However, it's history of reporting around the Apple Vision team has been spotty at best.

Apple Vision Pro and its development continue in spite of poor reporting on the product

Much of this report can be arrived at through simple conjecture based on Apple's previous strategies and already-announced features. The WWDC 2027 announcement date is new, though a second-half of 2027 launch window isn't.

There were several months where the publication reported that Apple's smart glasses are due in late 2026. Then suddenly, that shifted to late 2027 to align with other reports, though it cited internal struggles as usual.

The publication blames Apple's Siri AI launch delays and development snags, but that doesn't explain why everyone else had the currently agreed upon late 2027 release window. The publication has also run into repeated errors when reporting on Apple Vision Pro moves.

As with all rumors, it is best to remain skeptical.

items.title: Siri AI will be how Apple Glass will unseat Meta's smart glasses
items.content_html:
Apple's plan for its AI-equipped smart glasses is to lean on integrations with a user's existing iPhone apps, in a similar way to the CarPlay-like HomeView.

Apple's long-rumored smart glasses are expected to lean on AI processing for its first release. However, the way that it functions with AI will be key to their success.

Writing in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman says Apple is expecting app developers to prepare for the eventual introduction of its smart glasses in 2027.

However, rather than having apps running fully on the glasses, Apple wants developers to focus on Siri integrations. The aim is for specific functions within apps to be accessible to Siri, which can then be called upon by users wearing the glasses.

This is an approach that is similar to the rollout of HomeView. That device does not allow third-party apps to run directly, but it does let apps with existing CarPlay support to play audio and video.

For a device like smart glasses, this makes a lot of sense, especially if Apple keeps to its plan of making thin and light smart spectacles. It won't have enough onboard processing available to handle much in the way of apps.

That's something CarPlay and Siri AI solve by pushing the hard work to a nearby iPhone.

Winning through Siri AI

Apple's vision for the smart glasses will include Apple making a similar plea to developers to work on those elements before the launch of the Apple Vision Pro.

This push to use Siri AI is being performed with Apple believing it has the upper hand on current market dominator Meta. While Meta is entrenched in smart glasses, Apple's advantage comes from its pool of developers.

With a much larger pool of developers at its disposal in the App Store, as well as having worked on Siri integrations for the iPhone long beforehand, there should be little effort needed to make those Siri integrations work with the smart glasses.

With any luck, it should launch with a robust and vast number of things you can call upon Siri to do, without waiting for developers to catch up. All because the work had already been done.

items.title: Apple Glasses will not have Apple Vision Pro-style augmented reality
items.content_html:
Apple Glasses will not have Apple Vision Pro-style augmented reality

A report saying that Apple is preparing a new Apple Glasses type of headset, also says that they will not be like a lighter Apple Vision Pro.

In the short term, the expectation is that Apple will release its rumored AirPods update featuring sensors and cameras to register the environment around the wearer. Then Bloomberg says that those plus unspecified further sensors will be included in the glasses.

Reportedly, Apple employees are even referring to the glasses as "AirPods for your face." In the devices' first generation, these glasses will not present any visual data to the wearer.

So there'll be no in-vision data and no in-vision apps. What they will have is greater battery life than AirPods.

It's claimed that the battery life will be such that users can wear the Apple Glasses all day without recharging. Then, too, it should be easier for people to wear glasses in terms of comfort.

Such glasses should also be more acceptable in company than AirPods.

While there won't be any apps actually running on the Apple Glasses, there will be Siri AI. As well as responding to spoken commands, Siri AI in the glasses will be constantly receiving environmental information from the sensors.

Cameras and sensors

This report follows a recent supplier leak that appeared to confirm that Apple was working on both Apple Glasses and AirPods with cameras. It's still the case, though, that these cameras will not take photos.

Instead, they will provide sensors for AI and accessibility use. It's likely to be similar to how Siri Recap works now on the Apple Watch.

Rather than recording images, the cameras could provide data that is analyzed by Siri AI in real time. It sounds just like the way that Siri Recap does not record audio, yet is able to provide summaries of conversations.

So, perhaps, the cameras in Apple Glasses could detect an obstruction and Siri AI could verbally warn the wearer. That's already possible with an iPhone, since accessibility features such as door detection were added with iOS 16 back in 2022.
